name: Depressive realism
statement: Depressed people are said to judge their own control over events more accurately than everybody else, who hold a flattering illusion of control.
meaning: The claim comes in two strengths, and the literature has not always kept them apart. Moore and Fresco call the weaker one weak depressive realism: depressed people show less bias than non-depressed people, whether or not either group is accurate. The stronger one, which they call strong depressive realism, adds that depressed people show no bias at all, so their judgements sit on the objective value. Both versions are claims about a laboratory judgement, usually how much control a person believes they have over a light that comes on. Neither is a claim about seeing the world as it is.

origin.who: Lauren B. Alloy and Lyn Y. Abramson
origin.note: The paper is titled "Judgment of contingency in depressed and nondepressed students: Sadder but wiser?" and it does not contain the phrase "depressive realism" anywhere. The question mark in the title is the authors'.

evidence: Four experiments on University of Pennsylvania undergraduates, paid volunteers, who pressed or did not press a button across 40 trials and then rated how much control they had over a green light. Students scoring 9 or above on the Beck Depression Inventory went into the depressed group and 8 or below into the non-depressed group. Experiment 1, with 96 students and a real contingency in every problem, found no difference between the mood groups, and both groups were accurate. The famous result is Experiment 2, with 64 students and no contingency in either problem. Where the light came on 75% of the time, non-depressed women rated their control at 51.4 out of 100 against 13.1 for depressed women. The figures for men were 30.3 and 21.2. Experiment 3, also 64 students and also with no contingency, attached money to the light. Non-depressed students rated their control at 49.4 (men) and 64.4 (women) when winning, and at 6.9 and 21.2 when losing. Depressed men gave 17.2 and 21.2, depressed women 36.0 and 11.4, and the paper reports the depressed group's judgements as not differing between the two problems. Experiment 4, 64 students again, gave everyone real 50% control and varied whether money was won or lost. The non-depressed group judged it had less control in the losing problem than in the winning one, F(1, 48) = 19.60, p < .001, while the depressed group's judgements did not differ.

replication.headline: Pooled across 75 studies the effect sits below the conventional threshold for small, a 2026 meta-analysis of 151 samples finds the opposite sign, and a preregistered replication found no realism in either sample.
replication.detail: Moore and Fresco pooled 75 studies and 7,305 participants in 2012 and found a weighted mean d of -.07 in the direction depressive realism predicts. They call that below Cohen's convention for a small effect, which their table gives as .20. Trim and fill flagged four studies, and correcting for them moved the mean from -.09 to -.07. Both groups came out optimistic rather than one of them accurate, d = .14 for the dysphoric or depressed and d = .29 for the rest, which contradicts the strong version. Study effects ran from -3.59 to .99, Q = 493.89 on 74 degrees of freedom, p < .001. All three of their moderator hypotheses came out contrary to prediction. Studies with no objective standard of reality to compare judgements against produced d = -.15, against -.03 for studies that had one. Studies using self-report to measure depression produced d = -.04, while those using a structured clinical interview produced d = .16, the reverse of realism. External validity made almost no difference, d = -.03 for studies low on it and -.02 for studies high on it. The judgement-of-contingency task, where the effect was discovered, produced d = -.09, and within it depressed and non-depressed participants overestimated contingency to much the same degree, d = .53 and .60. Yeung, Lam and Chan pooled 130 articles and 151 samples in 2026, N = 33,043, and report a weak depressive distortion effect overall, Hedges's g = 0.09, with realism more likely on control or contingency tasks. Dev, Moore, Johnson and Garrett ran a preregistered replication in 2022, powered from the lower bound of the 90% interval around Alloy and Abramson's experiments 2 to 4, which called for 252. Sample One was 246 Amazon Mechanical Turk workers, part of them prescreened for symptom severity. Depression symptoms predicted more illusory control there, beta = 0.18, p < .001, the direction opposite to depressive realism, and the effect tracked anxious arousal rather than anhedonic depression. In an undergraduate second sample they did not predict it, beta = 0.05, p = .47.

study.cite: Dev, A. S., Moore, D. A., Johnson, S. L., & Garrett, K. T. (2022). Sadder ≠ Wiser: Depressive Realism Is Not Robust to Replication. Collabra: Psychology, 8(1), 38529.

limits: Moore and Fresco give standard deviations and fail-safe numbers around their pooled effects, and Dev and colleagues give standardised regression coefficients. No confidence interval was found around either headline figure in Moore and Fresco's text and tables or in the replication's results section, so none is quoted here. Yeung, Lam and Chan is paywalled and the figures above were read off its abstract at PubMed and at the publisher, not off the article. The studies here that used patients rather than students also fail to find the effect, and they fail differently. Carson, Hollon and Shelton found that patients with major depressive disorder underestimated control where control was real and were consistently more negative in their judgements. Venkatesh, Moulds and Mitchell tested 28 clinically depressed and 39 non-depressed participants and found every group showed the illusion of control. Msetfi and colleagues did obtain realism-shaped results, but only when long gaps separated the trials, and read that as depressed participants processing the context less rather than judging more accurately. Allan, Siegel and Hannah argue the pattern is a shift in willingness to predict the outcome rather than a difference in what people perceive, and they state that this response criterion analysis cannot be applied retrospectively to existing data. The 2022 paper gives its second sample as 134 in the abstract and 136 in the results text.
misreadings: The popular claim, that depression brings a clearer view of life, is far stronger than anything anybody has tested. What was measured is a rating of control over a light bulb across 40 trials. Alloy and Abramson's depressed group was students scoring 9 or above on a self-report inventory, not patients, and their Experiment 1 found no mood difference once the button actually controlled the light. Experiment 4 also gave real control and did find a difference, with the non-depressed group underestimating when the outcome was money lost. In Experiment 2 the overestimate was more pronounced among non-depressed women, and the problem-by-mood interaction was not significant for the men. Moore and Fresco's data undercut the accuracy framing directly, since dysphoric participants were optimistically biased too, just less so. And the reading that depression removes bias sits badly with the clinical findings, where depressed patients were wrong in a negative direction rather than right. The verdict on this page is about the contingency-judgement effect and its direct replication. Whether depressed people judge more accurately in general is a wider question, and Yeung, Lam and Chan's pooled estimate runs slightly the other way.
